Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time
When I think about the frightening event I can sometimes smell things that I smelt when the frightening event happened.

What happened to me was deeply unfair and nothing has been done about it
I feel dirty or contaminated because of what happened

The rest of the profile centers on bodily pain, terror, injustice, contamination, and identity change following interpersonal assault, so these two triggers appear clinically incoherent with the formulation and with the other selected items.

vignette:
Kofi has come to believe that his own kitchen is a hostile space. The final straw was last Tuesday evening, when a sliver of garlic, forgotten in the hot oil for a moment too long, sent a plume of acrid smoke into the air. The smell, sharp and stinging, was a key turning a lock in his mind. He was no longer in his quiet Chicago apartment but back in the flat he had shared with David six months ago. The same burnt smell filled his nostrils, thick and suffocating, just as it had that night when the pot of jollof rice had scorched on the stove, completely forgotten. With the smell came the memory, not as a thought but as a full-body reenactment. A phantom bloom of pain flared across his ribs, a dull, deep ache exactly where the kicks had landed. The terror was the most immediate part—a cold, paralyzing wave that started in his stomach and seized his lungs, the same helpless fear he felt when David, his breath sour with whiskey, had pinned him against the wall.

That night had been the end. The argument had started over something trivial, but it had twisted into something ugly when David, his voice slurring, had sneered, “You’re just like them, aren’t you? So weak, just like your family.” The comment about his family, who had sacrificed so much for him to build a life here, had been the spark. The violence that followed was a blur of motion and pain, punctuated by the smell of burnt rice and the overpowering scent of alcohol every time David shouted in his face. Now, standing in his own kitchen, Kofi dropped the pan into the sink with a clatter, his heart hammering against his ribs. He felt dirty, as if the memory itself had left a film on his skin that no amount of scrubbing could remove.

In the months since he left, Kofi has felt like a ghost haunting his own life. The man he was before—a confident curriculum designer, praised for his creative and engaging educational models—seems like a stranger to him now. He sees that former self in old photos, smiling easily, and feels a profound sense of loss. The person he has become is unrecognisable, a man who flinches at the smell of hand sanitizer at the office and who has to plan his route home from work to avoid walking past the bars where the scent of stale beer spills onto the sidewalk. He feels a constant, simmering anger at the injustice of it all. David faced no consequences. He was still out there, living his life, while Kofi was trapped in this sensory prison, ambushed by the smell of a colleague’s lunchtime whiskey-glaze salmon or a casual question about his family.

His work, once a source of pride, has become a struggle. During a brainstorming session last month, a coworker asked him about his family’s traditions to inform a module on cultural heritage. Kofi froze, David’s mocking words echoing in his head. He gave a clipped, noncommittal answer and spent the rest of the meeting staring at his laptop, the creative part of his brain feeling locked away and inaccessible. He has started declining all social invitations, especially after-work drinks, fabricating excuses that he knows sound flimsy to his colleagues. The isolation is a heavy blanket, but it feels safer than the risk of another memory ambush.

He decided to seek help after an incident at work where someone burned popcorn in the breakroom microwave. The smell flooded the open-plan office. For Kofi, it was the same acrid, choking scent from that night. He felt the terror rise, the ghost pain in his side so sharp he gasped. He could almost smell the whiskey on David’s breath again. He fled to the men’s room, locking himself in a stall and pressing his forehead against the cool metal, breathing through the panic until the shaking subsided. It was the public nature of the collapse, the sheer humiliation of his own reaction, that clarified things. He could not live like this anymore. He is not sure if the man he was is someone he can ever be again, but he holds onto a desperate hope that he can at least learn to feel clean again, to stand in his own kitchen without fear.
